name: Washo
confidence_why: Yu 2005 is the only source that states where Washo stress falls (on the stem's penultimate syllable, or on a final syllable with a long vowel), and Jacobsen's 1964 grammar, which treats stress as a phoneme and gives only stress-weakening rules rather than a placement rule, has example stems and a length-only-under-strong-stress restriction that fit Yu's rule, so the reading rests on one explicit statement that nothing contradicts.
catalog_citation: Yu, Alan C. L. 2005. Quantity, stress and reduplication in Washo. Phonology 22(3): 437-475. doi:10.1017/S0952675705000679 (author-posted publisher PDF,https://ayluna.github.io/images/Phonology22.pdf)
catalog_locator: p. 439 (sec. 2.1); pp. 443-446, sec. 3.1 'Stress assignment in Washo: some preliminaries', exx. (9)-(13), fn. 6, tableaux (15)-(16).
catalog_quote: [p. 439] Stress is assigned to stems and is generally on the penultimate syllable (see further discussion in §3.1). Long vowels are found only in stressed syllables. ... [p. 443] An examination of the available data reveals that stress is a property of the stem, which for the present purpose is defined maximally as a reduplicated root. Inflectional affixes generally do not receive stress. ... [p. 444] While main stress is generally on the penult (e.g. /ma'sat’i/ ‘flint arrowhead’; J84), it may surface on the final syllable if the final syllable contains a long vowel. (12) gu'ku: ‘owl sp.’ J84 mu'da:l ‘winnowing basket’ J90 dawma?'ga:p ‘wet place’ J90 t’u'gi:s ‘basket sp.’ J90 Su?'we:k ‘clam’ J413 Closed syllables do not in general attract stress, however. As shown below, main stress remains on the penult regardless of whether the antepenult (13a) or the final position (13b) contains a closed syllable. ... [p. 446] The importance of the Weight-to-Stress Principle is apparent when the input contains a long vowel. Main stress is on the last syllable, rather than the penult, since a candidate with penultimate stress would fatally violate WSP (16c). The final syllable can support a stressed foot since it is binary at the level of the mora.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Washo (isolate) is not in the catalog. Two title hits. (1) Yu 2005 (Phonology 22) is a first-hand, data-rich statement of Washo word stress: stress is a property of the stem, generally penultimate, final only when the final syllable has a long vowel, codas do not attract stress, inflectional affixes unstressed (sec. 3.1, pp. 443-445; open author copy already held by the project and re-read). This would ground a catalog record as weight-sensitive (vowel length only) stem-penultimate/right-edge stress. (2) Jacobsen 1973 'A rhythmic principle in Washo morphotactics' is an unpublished 1973 symposium paper; no copy located anywhere; the only characterisation found (Hanink 2021, LangSci 323 ch. 1 p. 7 fn. 7, open PDF saved) cites it for phonological conditioning of causative-affix placement, so it is prosody/morphotactics rather than a stress-placement source; low priority. Supporting material already held by the project from the earlier reading (Jacobsen 1964 grammar scan + selected scanned: stress is phonemic strong/weak, no placement rule given in ch. 1; Yu 2008 J. Phonetics p. 3 restates penultimate default with a small set of final-stress stems).

new_statements.rule_in_words: The stress domain is the stem (root plus plural reduplicant); inflectional prefixes and suffixes are outside it and unstressed. Main stress falls on the stem-penultimate syllable (a right-aligned trochee), so disyllabic roots are stressed on their first syllable and reduplicated stems keep stress on the new penult; if the stem-final syllable has a long vowel, stress is final instead (Weight-to-Stress). Closed syllables do not count as heavy for attracting stress. Every stressed syllable surfaces heavy: a short stressed vowel is followed by a lengthened (geminate) consonant, and long vowels occur only under stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; Yu's analysis has a single head foot (PARSE-σ ranked low) and Jacobsen 1964 recognises only strong vs weak stress (one strong stress per stem, pitch falling over following syllables, sec. 1.4 p.55).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress on stems whose last syllable has a long vowel (gu'ku: 'owl sp.', mu'da:l 'winnowing basket', dawma?'ga:p 'wet place', t'u'gi:s 'basket sp.', Su?'we:k 'clam'; Yu 2008 calls these 'a small subset of stems'). One lexical exception without a long vowel: se'sesm 'to vomit.PL' with final stress (fn. 6, possibly from post-tonic vowel deletion of /se'sesVm/). Jacobsen 1964 instead transcribes strong stress as a phoneme on each form and posits morphophonemic stress-weakening rules (secs. 3.18-3.20, not read).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem (root + reduplicant), not the inflected word: le-'?elel-i? 'my daughter's child' keeps root stress; le-?e'lelel-i? (plural) shifts to the reduplicated stem's penult. Data are Jacobsen 1964 citation forms (J-page refs) plus Yu's own fieldwork with Washo elders.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Washo (wash1253, ISO was) as a single language; Jacobsen 1964 (intro, text p.5) states dialect differences are minimal with a common phoneme inventory. Yu's data combine Jacobsen's 1950s-60s fieldwork (Woodfords CA, Dresslerville NV etc.) with his own 2000s recordings of elders; no separate dialect glottocode applies.

new_statements.reading: Washo word stress is stem-penultimate (domain = stem incl. reduplication, excluding inflectional affixes), overridden by final stress when the final syllable has a long vowel (weight-sensitive to vowel length only, not to codas); one lexical exception noted. Jacobsen 1964 (the primary grammar, sec. 1.4 p. 55, held by the project as scanned) only defines strong/weak stress phonemically and gives no placement rule, so Yu 2005 is the best explicit first-hand placement statement located.

new_statements.quote: [p.55, 1.4] Syllables with strong stress have greater intensity and higher pitch than do syllables with weak stress. In general the pitch falls gradually over the successive syllables following a strongly stressed syllable until it is again raised by the next strong stress or affected by an intonation. [p.312, 3.19] The stress weakener morphophoneme [symbol] brings it about that the next following vowel, which is always stressed on the morphophonemic level, is unstressed phonemically. [p.314, 3.20] When two stressed syllables occur in succession, the stress on the first syllable is generally weakened. Similarly, when two stressed syllables are separated by a syllable which loses its vowel by 3.15, the first stress is again weakened.

new_statements.relation_note: Jacobsen states no placement, so it neither confirms nor denies the Yu 2005 stem-penult/final-long-vowel rule that the existing statements record; his cited stems (émle, wáta, dó·ko, á·du, áŋal, ?émlu) are consistent with stem-penult stress. What it adds: stress is phonemic (strong/weak), lexically carried by stems and some affixes, length is confined to strongly stressed vowels, a juncture morphophoneme removes stress in auxiliary/exhortative/nominalized constructions, and adjacent-stress clash is resolved by weakening the first stress. The 'lexical (unpredictable)' reading is Jacobsen's structuralist analytic stance (stress as a phoneme marked per morpheme), not a claim against predictabi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jacobsen gives no positional placement rule. Stress is a two-way phoneme (strong vs weak, sec. 1.1/1.4); each morpheme carries its stress in the morphophonemic transcription (stems such as émle 'heart', wáta 'river', dó·ko 'heel', and suffixes such as -é·s Negative, -éwe? Resultative, -áša? Near Future, -á·ci Diminutive all carry underlying stress, pp. 260-261, 314). Surface stress is these lexical stresses minus two reductions: (i) the stress-weakener juncture (3.19) de-stresses the following underlyingly stressed vowel in auxiliary-verb derivation, the plural exhortative, and clause nominalization/adverbialization; (ii) clash (3.20): of two adjacent stressed syllables the first is 'generally' weakened, also when the intervening syllable has lost its vowel. Length occurs only after strongly stressed vowels (1.7.1, p. 57; 2.2, p. 82). The ch. 3 intro (p. 255) confirms these two sections are the whole treatment of stress: 'stress is treated in sections 3.19-3.20'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None as such: only a strong/weak contrast is set up (1.1, p. 52); the alternative 'long stress' analysis (1.7.1) is a merger of strong stress and length, not a secondary degree. Words may contain more than one strong stress (e.g. 3.19 examples), reduced only by the clash rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Clash weakening is stated as 'generally', not absolute; one example is tagged to a single informant (BH). The stress weakener applies only in the three named constructions. No lexical exceptions to a placement rule are listed because no placement rule is given.
new_statements.identity_note: Jacobsen's data are from Washo speakers of Carson Valley / Dresslerville, Nevada (first informant Hank Pete of Dresslerville; intro pp. 23, 41); he states that 'the dialectal differences are minimal, and there is no clearly delineated boundary of speech types' and that the phoneme inventory is common to all speakers encountered (intro, p. 23), so the stress description is for Washo generally, with a few forms tagged by informant initials.

readall_conflicts: No data conflict. Jacobsen 1964 treats stress as a phoneme carried by individual morphemes and gives only reduction rules (stress-weakener juncture, clash weakening of the first of two adjacent stresses), never a placement rule; Yu 2005 (already the catalog's statement of record) derives placement as stem-penultimate, final if the final stem syllable has a long vowel, inflectional affixes unstressed. These differ in analytic framing (structuralist phonemic stress vs predictable metrical stress), and Jacobsen's own example stems fit Yu's generalization, so the overall reading stays with Yu 2005 (weight-sensitive, stem-penult) with Jacobsen's clash/juncture rules as added detail.

sources.citation: Yu, Alan C. L. 2008. The phonetics of quantity alternation in Washo. Journal of Phonetics 36(3): 508-520. doi:10.1016/j.wocn.2007.10.004
sources.quote: Previous phonological studies have proposed that syllables bearing stress in Washo must be phonologically heavy (i.e., (C)V: or (C)VC). This paper shows the phonetic correlates of this phonological claim. [p. 2] ... Long vowels are found only in stressed syllables; short vowels can occur in any syllable. Stress is assigned to stems and is generally on the penultimate syllable, although a small subset of stems has final stress [...]. When stress is final, the tonic vowel is invariable long. [p. 3]
sources.locator: pp. 2-3 (author-posted in-press pagination; sec. 0 and sec. 1 'Quantity alternation in Washo'); results pp. 5-10, conclusion p. 10
sources.note: Sec. 2 background: 'Long vowels are found only in stressed syllables; short vowels can occur in any syllable. Stress is assigned to stems and is generally on the penultimate syllable, although a small subset of stems has final stress (e.g., mudá:l 'winnowing basket'; šuʔwé:k 'clam'). When stress is final, the tonic vowel is invariabl[y] long.' Instrumental study of post-tonic consonant lengthening after short stressed vowels (stress-to-weight).
